title: A fiery sky over Paranal
caption: A reddened twilight sky over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
captureDate: Six months after the eruption of 15 January 2022
captureShort: Six months after the eruption of 15 January 2022
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: An unusually red twilight glows above the dark silhouette of Cerro Paranal, where ESO's Very Large Telescope points up at the sky beneath the Milky Way. The colour has a dramatic cause: a volcanic eruption thousands of kilometres away.

On 15 January 2022 the southern Pacific Ocean saw the undersea volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha‘apai erupt. Its shock waves spread through the atmosphere, and weather stations at ESO's Paranal and La Silla observatories, more than 10 000 kilometres away, recorded the disturbance.

The eruption also threw an ash plume 57 kilometres high, loading the atmosphere with particles such as water vapour and dust. Tiny dust particles scatter sunlight and make it redder, an effect several ESO telescopes picked up in their twilight calibration images. This photo was taken 6 months after the eruption, showing that the effect lasted well beyond the event itself.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way appears more strongly against the red twilight than it would to someone watching.

explore: By the time ESO published the picture, a year after the eruption, the sky had still not returned to the state it was in before the volcano erupted, a sign of how long such fine particles can linger high above the ground.
alt: A deep red twilight sky with the Milky Way above the dark outline of a mountain topped by telescope buildings.
